name: Cache/timing side-channel attack analysis and constant-time fix
theory_paragraphs: A \term{side channel} is a \imp{passive, non-invasive attack} that observes physical byproducts of execution --- time, cache state, power, sound --- instead of breaking the algorithm itself. In information-flow terms: classify variables as \term{high} (secret) vs \term{low} (public); \term{non-interference} demands that two states equal on low variables produce indistinguishable executions. Even when the \emph{outputs} are equal, a cache/timing side channel breaks this because the \emph{executions} remain distinguishable through the observation channel. Hardware facts that matter: caches are \imp{transparent, shared, and subject to collisions}; a \term{cache miss} costs much more time than a hit; data moves in fixed-size \term{lines} (typically 64 bytes).

The three attacker models, in increasing power: \begin{tightitem} \item \term{time-driven}: the attacker measures total execution time, which is a function of the number of cache hits/misses (e.g. ``more than one miss implies secret $\neq 0$''). \item \term{access-driven}: the attacker flushes or primes the cache before the victim runs, then observes \emph{which lines} were touched or evicted (prime-and-probe; reloads of primed lines are timed). Requires shared memory or co-residency. \item \term{trace-driven}: the attacker profiles the per-operation hit/miss trace (e.g. Miss-Miss-Hit vs Miss-Hit-Miss reveals a taken branch). \end{tightitem} For a direct-mapped cache with $N$ lines of $L$ bytes and an array with $b$-byte entries, entry $i$ sits in line $\lfloor i \cdot b / L \rfloor \bmod N$; two data items mapping to the same line \imp{evict each other}, so only one is cached at a time.

\term{Countermeasures} form a spectrum: \begin{tightitem} \item \term{Constant-time programming}: never branch on a secret and use only secret-independent memory indices (e.g. branchless select $r = b \cdot x + (1-b) \cdot y$). \item \term{Cache normalization}: flush the cache at entry/exit, or preload (prime) every line the program might use so the footprint is secret-independent; alternatively pad execution to worst-case execution time. \item \term{Reduce bandwidth}: add noise (random dummy accesses), reduce timer precision, partition/color the cache per process, randomize data layout ($M[\pi(i)]$ or $\&M' = \&M + r$). \end{tightitem}

Under \term{speculative execution}, instructions on a mispredicted branch path execute \term{transiently} and can still fetch lines into the cache (stores are not committed). A Spectre-v1-style leak needs \imp{two gadgets}: a \term{reading gadget} (a transient load that overreads a secret, e.g. an out-of-bounds index after a mispredicted bounds check) and a \term{transmitting gadget} (a second access whose address depends on the read value, encoding it into the cache state, later recovered by prime-and-probe). The attacker poisons the branch predictor to steer speculation. A reading gadget alone discloses nothing. Defenses: serialization (\texttt{lfence} after the branch), index masking (SLH: mask the index with the comparison result), or hardware with non-speculative cache effects / taint tracking.
theory_cheatsheet: Line of entry $i$: $\lfloor i \cdot b / L \rfloor \bmod N_{lines}$; entries sharing a line evict each other (direct-mapped).
Only indices, branches, or loop bounds that depend on a \term{secret} can leak; public/constant indices never leak.
Time-driven $=$ count misses from execution time; access-driven $=$ flush/prime, then record touched lines.
One execution leaks at most a predicate (1 bit); sweeping an attacker input over all values upgrades the leak to the exact secret (line boundaries pin the secret's residue).
Fix must match the leak: branchless select for secret branches, preload/flush all possibly-used lines for secret indices.
Speculation adds leakage only with \emph{both} a reading gadget and a transmitting gadget; $\bmod$-guarded indices cannot overread.
identify_givens: A stated cache geometry (total size, number of lines, bytes per line, direct-mapped, data cache only), an array/table layout saying which entries map to which cache line, a short C-like victim program with secret variables (e.g. A, B, C) and possibly an attacker-controlled public input (e.g. D), and an attacker model: time-driven (execution time depends only on the number of cache misses/hits) or access-driven (attacker observes which cache lines are touched or evicted, possibly over repeated runs with chosen inputs).
identify_target: Explain why the program is insecure and name the leaking instructions; show how the attacker correlates multiple executions (varying the public input) to recover a secret value, range, or predicate; propose a concrete fix (constant-time/branchless rewrite or cache preloading/flushing); and sometimes judge whether speculative execution (branch prediction) increases the leakage.
strategy_name: Map lines, flag secret-dependent accesses, correlate runs, then make the footprint secret-independent

algorithm.detail: From the geometry compute the line of every datum: entry $i$ of an array with $b$-byte entries and $L$-byte lines sits in line $\lfloor i \cdot b / L \rfloor \bmod N_{lines}$ (often $b=4$, $L=64$, so 16 entries per line). Note collisions: \imp{two regions mapping to the same line evict each other}, so only one can be cached at a time. Also record which line holds the scalar secret/public variables.

Mark every instruction whose \begin{tightitem} \item memory index, \item branch condition, or \item iteration count \end{tightitem} depends on a secret --- directly (\texttt{M[A]}) or mixed with attacker input (\texttt{M[(B+D) mod 64]}). These are the \imp{only possible leak sources}; accesses with public or constant indices never leak.

\term{Time-driven}: count cache misses per execution, simulating the direct-mapped cache line by line (a miss occurs when the needed line differs from the resident one; colliding regions can make the count constant --- check!). \term{Access-driven}: assume the attacker flushes/primes the cache before each run and records the set of lines touched (or evicted) after it.

Enumerate the attacker-controlled input values and tabulate the observed line set or miss count for each. Subtract what the attacker already knows (constant lines, lines of public indices like $\lfloor D/16 \rfloor$); the residual variation is a function of the secret: e.g. observing line $\lfloor ((B+D) \bmod 64)/16 \rfloor$ while sweeping $D$ pins down $B$ exactly (the run where the observed line jumps reveals $B \bmod 16$, the line number reveals $\lfloor B/16 \rfloor$). State precisely what is recovered: \imp{exact value, range, or one predicate bit}.

Match the fix to the flagged instruction from Step 2: \begin{tightitem} \item secret-dependent branch / loop bound $\rightarrow$ \term{constant-time code}: fixed loop bounds, always execute both sides, select with arithmetic $r = b \cdot x + (1-b) \cdot y$; \item secret-dependent array index $\rightarrow$ \term{cache normalization}: preload (or flush) all possibly-used lines first, e.g. read \texttt{M[0], M[16], M[32], M[48]}, so the cache footprint is identical for every secret. \end{tightitem}

Under branch prediction, instructions on a mispredicted path may execute transiently and still fetch their lines into the cache --- a \term{reading gadget} (a speculative overread only if the index is unbounded; a $\bmod$-guarded index cannot overread). But leakage additionally needs a \term{transmitting gadget} that encodes the loaded value into the cache state. \imp{Reading gadget alone discloses nothing}; conclude accordingly.

variations.name: Time-driven vs access-driven on the same program
variations.detail: The professor swaps the attacker model and the answer flips. Under time-driven counting, colliding arrays can make the miss count \emph{constant} for straight-line code (trap: do not claim leakage there), while a secret-dependent branch still leaks one bit via one extra miss. Under access-driven observation with no shared memory, the same program may leak nothing because the same lines are always evicted; with shared memory the attacker can tell which array is resident. \imp{Always redo Step 3 for the stated model} instead of reusing conclusions.

variations.name: Single-run boolean leak vs multi-run exact recovery
variations.detail: Sometimes there is no attacker input (dasak18: only secrets A, B, C) --- then one execution leaks at most a predicate (e.g. ``B true causes one extra miss''). When the attacker controls an input $D$ and may rerun (exam P8), the secret-dependent index $(B+D) \bmod 64$ sweeps across the lines as $D$ varies, upgrading the leak from a range to the \imp{exact value} of $B$. Adapt Step 4: without a knob, tabulate the branch cases; with a knob, sweep all its values.

variations.name: Wrong-fix trap: branchless vs preloading
variations.detail: The fix must match the flagged instruction from Step 2. A branchless select $a \mathrel{+}= B \cdot A_1 + (1-B) \cdot A_2$ fixes a secret-dependent \emph{branch} but does nothing for a secret-dependent \emph{array index}; preloading all lines fixes index leakage but not a secret-dependent loop bound. Answers proposing the mismatched fix lose points.

variations.name: Speculation sub-question with gadget reasoning
variations.detail: A final part asks whether speculative execution leaks more. Expected two-part reasoning: transient loads on a mispredicted path can fill lines (and an unbounded index like \texttt{M[D]} with $D \geq 64$ is a speculative \term{overread}, unlike the $\bmod\, 64$-guarded one), but without a \term{transmitting gadget} no extra information is disclosed. Trap: answering ``Spectre, so yes it leaks'' without separating reading gadget from transmitter.

original_problem: A system has a direct-mapped data cache (no instruction cache) of 512 bytes: 8 lines of 64 bytes each. Arrays \texttt{A} and \texttt{B} each hold 32 public entries of 4 bytes. \texttt{A[i]} maps to line $\lfloor i/16 \rfloor \in \{0,1\}$, and \texttt{B} is placed so that \texttt{B[i]} maps to the \emph{same} line $\lfloor i/16 \rfloor$: the two arrays collide on lines 0 and 1, so an \texttt{A}-block and a \texttt{B}-block can never be cached simultaneously. The scalars \texttt{u}, \texttt{v}, \texttt{r}, \texttt{q} share one 64-byte block mapped to line 2. \texttt{u} is secret with $0 \leq u < 32$; \texttt{v} is a secret boolean, $v \in \{0,1\}$; \texttt{r} is a local variable; \texttt{q} is public and controlled by the attacker, $0 \leq q < 32$. The victim program is: (1) \texttt{r = 0}; (2) \texttt{r += A[u]}; (3) \texttt{if (v == 1) \{} (4) \texttt{r += B[q]}; \texttt{\} else \{} (5) \texttt{r += A[q]}; \texttt{\}}. The attacker runs a \emph{time-driven} attack: the cache is empty before each execution, he may rerun the program with the same secrets and any \texttt{q} of his choice, and he measures total execution time, which grows strictly with the number of cache misses. (a) Explain why the program is not secure and state exactly which instructions leak. (b) Show how the attacker correlates the timings over his chosen \texttt{q} values, and state precisely what he learns about \texttt{v} and about \texttt{u}. (c) Rewrite the program in constant-time style so that the miss count no longer depends on the secrets, and verify that the count is the same for all \texttt{u}, \texttt{v}, \texttt{q}. Explain also why preloading both arrays is impossible here. (d) Suppose the CPU predicts the branch on line 3 and executes the not-taken side speculatively. Can the attacker learn more about the secrets than in (b)? Justify using the notions of reading and transmitting gadgets.

original_steps.work: Line size 64 B with 4-byte entries gives $64/4 = 16$ entries per line, so \texttt{A[i]} and \texttt{B[i]} both sit in line $\lfloor i/16 \rfloor \in \{0,1\}$; the \texttt{A}-block and the \texttt{B}-block of the same line evict each other. The scalars sit on line 2, which collides with nothing used by the program.

Line 2 (\texttt{r += A[u]}) has a memory index depending directly on the secret \texttt{u}. Line 3 (\texttt{if (v == 1)}) is a branch on the secret \texttt{v}: it decides \emph{whether} line 4 (\texttt{B[q]}) or line 5 (\texttt{A[q]}) executes, so the cache footprint of lines 4--5 depends on a secret even though the index \texttt{q} itself is public. These are the only leak sources; line 1 touches only the constant scalar line 2.

Time-driven model, cache initially empty. Every run starts with 1 miss for the scalar line 2 and 1 miss for \texttt{A[u]} on line 2 (instruction 2), which loads the \texttt{A}-block of line $\lfloor u/16 \rfloor$. \begin{tightitem} \item Case $v = 1$: \texttt{B[q]} needs the \texttt{B}-block of line $\lfloor q/16 \rfloor$. That block is never resident (the line is either cold or holds the \texttt{A}-block, which is a different block), so it always misses: total $= 3$ misses for every $q$. \item Case $v = 0$: \texttt{A[q]} hits iff the \texttt{A}-block of line $\lfloor q/16 \rfloor$ is resident, i.e. iff $\lfloor q/16 \rfloor = \lfloor u/16 \rfloor$. Total $= 2$ misses if $\lfloor q/16 \rfloor = \lfloor u/16 \rfloor$, else $3$. \end{tightitem}

The attacker sweeps all $q \in \{0, \dots, 31\}$ and records which runs are fast (2 misses). (i) If some value $q^{\ast}$ gives a fast run, then $v = 0$ (fast runs never occur when $v = 1$) and $\lfloor u/16 \rfloor = \lfloor q^{\ast}/16 \rfloor$, so $u$ is pinned to the 16 candidates $\{16\ell, \dots, 16\ell + 15\}$ with $\ell = \lfloor q^{\ast}/16 \rfloor$. (ii) If every $q$ gives 3 misses, then $v = 1$: were $v = 0$, the sweep would include a $q$ in \texttt{u}'s line (both lines contain attacker-chosen indices), producing a fast run. So $v$ is recovered \emph{exactly} in all cases; $u$ is narrowed to its line (16 candidates) when $v = 0$ and remains completely unknown (32 candidates) when $v = 1$.

Constant-time rewrite (branchless select, unconditional accesses): (1) \texttt{r = 0}; (2) \texttt{r += A[u]}; (3) \texttt{t1 = B[q]}; (4) \texttt{t2 = A[q]}; (5) \texttt{r += v*t1 + (1-v)*t2};. Verification of the miss count: scalar line 1 miss; \texttt{A[u]} 1 miss; \texttt{B[q]} always 1 miss (its block is never resident); \texttt{A[q]} always 1 miss, because \texttt{B[q]} has just loaded the \texttt{B}-block of line $\lfloor q/16 \rfloor$, and the colliding \texttt{A}-block cannot be resident at the same time. Total $= 4$ misses for \emph{every} $u, v, q$ --- the timing is secret-independent. The multiplication by \texttt{v} is data-oblivious arithmetic, not a branch. Note that preloading cannot work here: \texttt{A} and \texttt{B} collide on lines 0--1, so no cache state can hold both arrays; eliminating the secret-dependent \emph{branch} (not normalizing the cache) is the fix that matches the leak.

On a misprediction of line 3 the not-taken side executes transiently; its load (\texttt{B[q]} or \texttt{A[q]}) may fetch or evict lines but is not committed. This adds no information: \begin{tightitem} \item no \term{reading gadget} on a secret --- the only transiently executed index is the public \texttt{q}; the secret-indexed load \texttt{A[u]} lies on the always-executed path and is not amplified by speculation; \item no \term{transmitting gadget} --- no access has an address depending on a transiently read value, so nothing encodes a secret into the cache state. \end{tightitem} Speculation can at worst perturb the timings (a transient fetch costs an extra miss), but it discloses nothing beyond part (b).
